Thanks again for the demo today — the team liked the latency and the retriever integration. Two quick follow-ups from our side before we loop procurement:

1) Can you confirm exactly what we should be measuring for "units"? We heard tokens, characters, and requests thrown around and want to map this to our billing model. Our current telemetry is in characters.
2) We need a ballpark target for $/1M tokens so we can map to our budget range (target is roughly $40k–$120k/year for this feature).
3) How does prompt caching affect what we would actually be billed? If we cache a common prefix across users, do those cached tokens still show up on our bill?

Rough expected activity: 350k API calls/month, average prompt ~1,200 characters, average completion ~400 characters. Happy for you to translate these to tokens.

From: hannah_schmitt <hannah@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Demo + pricing follow-up (pricing units + caching explainer)

Liam — thanks for the clear list. Quick recap and concrete mappings below so procurement has numbers to work with. High level: Redwood bills by tokens (prompt + completion). Characters and requests are proxies you can use for estimation but they are not the billing unit.

Short answers up front:
- Billing unit: tokens (we charge per 1K billed tokens).
- Characters -> tokens: average English text is ~4 characters per token (so tokens ~= characters / 4). Use that to convert your telemetry.
- Requests: count of API calls — important for concurrency/throughput and burst planning, not directly a billing unit unless you have request-based metering on a custom plan.
- Prompt caching: when a prompt prefix is served from a cache with a 100% hit, you do not pay for re-processing those prefix tokens (they are not billed); you still pay for completion tokens that the model generates. Cache effectiveness reduces billed prompt tokens and therefore reduces cost.

Worked example using your numbers (convert characters -> tokens using /4):
- Avg prompt 1,200 chars -> ~300 tokens prompt.
- Avg completion 400 chars -> ~100 tokens completion.
- Per call billed tokens ~= 400 tokens.
- 350k calls/month * 400 tokens = 140,000,000 tokens/month.
- Per-1M token buckets: 140 * 1M tokens/month.

Unit economics (illustrative):
- If price = $90 / 1M tokens -> monthly = 140 * $90 = $12,600.
- If price = $40 / 1M tokens -> monthly = 140 * $40 = $5,600.
- If price = $150 / 1M tokens -> monthly = 140 * $150 = $21,000.

Now factor caching: if you can cache a 50% prefix-hit rate on the prompts, billed prompt tokens drop to ~150 per call, so billed tokens per call ~= 250 -> monthly tokens = 87.5M -> multiply by price/$1M to get the new monthly cost. That delta is where caching creates material savings.

Next steps I propose:
- I'm attaching a short pricing cheat sheet (redwood-pricing-cheatsheet.pdf) and a quick conversion spreadsheet — I can populate it with your exact telemetry if you share a sample CSV (you mentioned you could provide usage).
- Dylan (cc) — can you add notes on batching/throughput and any throughput-related constraints for 350k calls/month (esp. peak QPS) and whether we should recommend Dedicated vs Hosted?
- Liam — if this looks right, we'll produce a 1–2 page commercial estimate for procurement and a proposed PO flow.

Thanks — Hannah
Hannah Schmitt
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood-pricing-cheatsheet.pdf (1 page)

Subject: Re: Demo + pricing follow-up (throughput + batching)

Nice summary, Hannah. Two technical notes to complement the cost calc:

- Batching: our runtime can batch many short requests together which reduces GPU overhead. Batching helps most when requests are frequent and short; with 350k calls/month the benefit depends heavily on arrival distribution (peak QPS). If you expect spikes (e.g., Black Friday), batching will help average cost but you still need headroom for latency SLOs.
- KV/Prefix cache semantics: cache hits avoid re-encoding the cached prefix on the model; that means the runtime does not re-run those prompt tokens on the GPU and they are not billed. However, some telemetry (logs) will still show the original prompt for audit — billing is based on tokens the model actually processes during inference.

I recommend two pragmatic steps so we can give procurement a narrow band:
1) Send the sample CSV of real request-level telemetry (we can accept a small extract). I'll run a quick conversion script (chars->tokens) and produce a per-month estimated token burn with and without caching assumptions.
2) If Acme wants predictable unit economics, we can propose a committed Dedicated capacity quote (reduces per-1M token price and gives SLA). Otherwise hosted pay-as-you-go numbers work but have more variance.

Happy to run the file when you send it.

—Dylan
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
